items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-08-23
items.q: Coon Kent Joan up on the South Street in the back of his club. He and Fast Life Eddie, Treacherous Slim, Big Dipper. I'm trying to think of some of the guys, the Whispering Boots. All those guys were big-time gamblers.

ctx.x: Did that cause the demise of that club? Because I don't think it...

I don't think so. No. No. I don't think it caused the demise of the club. I think things started changing with... You see, Club Desire was down in the Ninth Ward. But you had the Dewdrop, the Robin Hood, and all of these Johnny-come-lately clubs, which were just beginning to hit their stride to develop new entertainment. Then, like I said, you had the Coliseum Arena, which was in the central part of the city. You had the ILA Club, which was in the French Quarter. You had all of these things jumping against…
How do you see the difference? Is there any difference between rhythm and blues and rock and roll? I mean, did you see a difference?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: Whispering Boots belonged to that era that we discussed sometime with Fast Life Eddie, Big Coochie, Treacherous Slim, Bulldog Jackson, Midnight Willie, Deep Dick Johnny. All these guys were big-time pimps

ctx.x: Well, Whispering Boots belonged to that era that we discussed sometime with Fast Life Eddie, Big Coochie, Treacherous Slim, Bulldog Jackson, Midnight Willie, Deep Dick Johnny. All these guys were big-time pimps, and they had women of the evening where you could go to the little, in the little alleys where they had these little motels or little small rooms. And this was before they could go to the downtown hotels. All this is a part of the jazz era of music, the way black people lived at that particular time. And…
This is also from the Pittsburgh Courier. This is about that. It's from November 7, 1953 of the Pittsburgh Courier. And so maybe you could read it. It's just a little article.
